They Say SEMA Is Wild, This 700-HP Chevy S10 Hellcat Street Truck Runs Mid-Sevens (There's a Catch)
49 photos
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious
Chevrolet’s light-duty pickup peak in engine size arrived with the 1990 C1500 454 SS, a 7.4-liter V8 bruiser wheezing out 230 horsepower for 15.7-second quarter-mile passes, while modern 6.2-liter Silverado 1500 trucks deliver 420 horsepower and 14.1-second sprints. Sadly, General Motors repeatedly failed to drop a Hemi V8 into its pickups. Corporate copyright infringement laws stop executives, leaving everyday gearheads limited strictly by their wallets. Meet the Chevy S10 Hellcat.
Before somebody yelled “hold my beer” and grabbed a welding torch, the humble Chevrolet S10 spent two generations hauling bags of garden mulch between 1982 and 2004. The first generation ran from 1982 to 1993, followed by a sleeker second generation from 1994 to 2004. For buyers craving factory rebellion with a bowtie badge, Chevrolet offered the 1994 to 1998 S10 SS and the ground-hugging 1999 to 2003 S10 Xtreme.
Those sporty Chevrolets packed a 4.3-liter Vortec V6 paired with either a 4L60-E 4-speed automatic or NV3500 5-speed manual transmission, mustering a polite 195 horsepower and 260 lb-ft of torque for a 7.8-second 0-to-60 mph jog and a 16.1-second quarter-mile at 86 mph. General Motors only went truly unhinged with the 1991 to 1992 GMC Syclone cousin, whose turbocharged 4.3-liter V6 made 280 horsepower for 13.4-second quarter-mile blasts.
Meanwhile, over at Chrysler’s asylum, engineers birthed the supercharged 6.2-liter Gen III Hemi V8, famous as the Hellcat, for the 2015 model year, retiring it from muscle cars in 2023 while keeping utility vehicles screaming through 2026. Force-fed by a 2.4-liter twin-screw supercharger, it initially unleashed 707 horsepower and 650 lb-ft of torque in the Dodge Challenger, Charger , and Jeep Grand Cherokee Trackhawk, before standard Dodge models hit 717 horsepower.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Mopar stuffed that rowdy mill everywhere, rating it at 702 horsepower in the Ram 1500 TRX and 710 horsepower in the Dodge Durango, while 2.7-liter supercharged Redeye, Super Stock, and Jailbreak models delivered 797 to 807 horsepower. Following the 840-horsepower 2018 Demon, the 1,025-horsepower 2023 Challenger SRT Demon 170 clocked a neck-snapping 1.66-second 0 to 60 mph launch and an 8.91-second quarter-mile, while a 707-horsepower Mopar Hellcrate retails for $20,215.
In 2024, Victor Rafael, the mastermind behind the VICtorious and G2K Youtube channels, looked at his black first-generation S10 pickup, ironically nicknamed Sleepy Joe, and decided humanity had suffered enough predictable LS swaps. Craving 707 horsepower of supercharged Mopar blasphemy in a featherweight Chevy, Victor yanked the truck’s old LS V8 and 2-speed Powerglide, then hired Tom Kozlow, alias Street Racing Tom, to build a Turbo 400 3-speed automatic.
Forcing a Mopar engine to marry a General Motors gearbox required an SFI-certified J&W Performance adapter bellhousing. Next, the factory front-sump Hemi oil pan threatened to smash the S10 steering linkage, and since Victor refused to tube the front frame, he snagged a scarce Holley Gen III Hemi rear-sump pan from Summit Racing. With the doghouse removed, buddy Steve and fabricator Charles of Solo Man Motorsport wrestled the beast inside.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Because massive Hemi cylinder heads left 0 inches of vertical wiggle room, lifting the engine 2 inches off standard clamshell mounts for removal was impossible. Instead, Charles modified Paul Horton’s Welder Series mounts with stationary rear tabs and bolt-in front plates, letting the V8 slide straight forward off the transmission dowels. Charles also inverted and plated the stock transmission crossmember bracket, while a shop shortened the driveshaft to 54.5 inches.
When the rear supercharger water manifold collided with the cab, Victor skipped buying a $429.95 Earl’s 1.875-inch manifold and introduced his firewall to an angle grinder, welding in custom sheet metal coated with primer, seam sealer, and satin black paint. Bulky SRT exhaust manifolds failed to fit, so he bought $329.95 Hooker Blackheart Hemi swap headers with V-band clamps and added Speedway Motors tubular upper arms with 1.5-inch ball joints.
Steering demanded creativity after the driver-side valve cover evicted the stock column pocket. Victor installed a modified TRZ Motorsports race column with a Delrin bushing, U-joints snaking past the header to the factory gearbox, a Strange quick-disconnect hub, and a Grant wheel. Up front, he trimmed 1 inch off the core support to fit an oversized radiator, dual electric fans, Gates hoses, and an oil cooler with a 90-degree adapter.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Out in the bed beside two nitrous bottles, a Mitsubishi radiator, custom fan shroud, and intercooler pump push water through 0.75-inch lines to chill the blower. A rear fuel cell feeds stock rails via a MagnaFuel ProTuner 750 pump, Jegs 100-micron filter, E85-ready Evil Energy PTFE lines, Redhorse regulator, and Low Doller sensor. Electronics include a Holley Terminator X Max ECU, drive-by-wire Hemi pedal, vacuum block, and SmoothBoost bypass controller.
After Victor notched the frame for a 1-wire alternator, added a 3D-printed SR10 grille badge made by Mike from Backyard Shenanigans, and installed a 2006 to 2010 Charger mini-starter, the starter missed the flywheel. Shaving the starter face took 1 week and $120 at a machine shop. Worse, when the engine fired on a tune from Mike at Sinister Performance Club, it showed zero oil pressure from a trashed crankshaft.
Refusing to cry into his toolbox, Victor bought a refreshed 6.2-liter Hellcat engine making over 700 horsepower from Mike at Sinister Performance Club, while California wizard Richard Nedbal of FastManEFI assisted with calibration. On his birthday, Victor trailered Sleepy Joe on meaty Hoosier drag radials to Florida’s Immokalee Regional Raceway for a no-prep shootout, yanking both front wheels skyward, pedaling through ferocious tire smoke, and clocking a 7.50-second eighth-mile pass.
